summary:
Limpopo is a province of the Republic of South Africa and stands under the national legal framework; the province-specific material in the source inventory concerns the reach of customary law and traditional authority in rural districts that formed part of the former Bantustans.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 May 2012 that the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament would create a parallel customary-law justice system covering people living in the former Bantustans, with no provision allowing anyone to opt out of its jurisdiction. The same account records that rural LGBT people already faced discrimination, violence and poor cooperation from police, and that chiefs' courts in rural areas punished lesbians.

A commentary published by Mamba Online on 18 April 2012 by Melanie Judge, written while the bill was being debated in provincial public hearings, described the proposed separate customary system as one that would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas. It reported that lesbians were punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, that the bill offered no opt-out, and that those able to leave rural areas were expected to do so. Traditional leaders also opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.

For a trans visitor, the exposure described is concentrated in rural districts where customary forums operate: a person whose presentation or relationship is read as non-conforming in those settings faces a forum with no opt-out and documented hostility from traditional authorities, alongside weak police response to complaints.
tangentialFactors:
The bill's coverage was defined by the former Bantustans rather than by provincial boundaries, so its incidence in Limpopo depends on the extent of that territory within the province. The sources treat former-Bantustan areas as a category spanning several provinces, which makes Limpopo one instance of a wider pattern rather than a separately documented case.

The tension the sources describe runs between customary authority and national recognition law rather than between Limpopo and the national framework: traditional leaders' opposition to the Civil Union Act of 2006 is recorded as a position of traditional leadership, not of the provincial government.
localsOnly:
Residents of Limpopo's rural districts who are subject to customary jurisdiction have no opt-out under the bill as described, and those who can leave rural areas are expected to do so.

Punishment of lesbians is recorded as taking place at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices, and rural LGBT residents are recorded as facing discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation.

Traditional leaders in the province opposed the Civil Union Act of 2006.
outOfScopeNotes:
Both sources date from 2012 and describe a bill then before parliament. The inventory does not establish whether that bill was enacted, lapsed or replaced, so the current legal status of customary jurisdiction in Limpopo is unresolved on these sources.

No Limpopo-specific enforcement data is present: there are no provincial figures on prosecutions, hate-crime reporting, police conduct complaints or violence against trans residents, and no provincial information on identity-document processing, health-care access or facilities rules.

The two sources are an international human rights organisation and a domestic LGBT news publication, and their characterisation of the bill's effect on LGBT people in rural areas is their own assessment rather than a court finding.
